idiom_name: one driver transaction per business operation (knex.transaction / pg client / Prisma callback)
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the dominant stacks expose the boundary and nothing more: node-postgres expects BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK issued through the same client (and warns that transactions must not use pool.query), Knex hands the callback a promise-aware transaction handle and commits on resolve or rolls back on reject, and Prisma's db.transaction(tx => ...) commits when the callback returns and rolls back when it throws. That callback is the idiomatic unit of work in JavaScript: collect what must be written, perform every write through the transaction-scoped handle, and let the callback's outcome decide commit or rollback - there is no separate register/flush object. MikroORM is the exception that ships the classic structure (identity map, UnitOfWork with snapshot diffing, em.flush()) and is available as a variant.
pitfalls: Using pool.query (or a second client) for statements inside the transaction silently escapes it - every statement must go through the same client or trx handle.
The transaction handle must be threaded through every helper; a helper that opens its own connection commits separately and cannot be rolled back.
Side effects inside the callback (emails, queue pushes, cache writes) survive a rollback, so they belong after the transaction resolves.
A transaction that is never committed or rolled back holds its connection and locks until the process releases it.

variants.name: MikroORM UnitOfWork (identity map + snapshot diffing + em.flush())
variants.idiom_name: EntityManager + UnitOfWork: persist() then flush() inside an implicit transaction
variants.implementation_notes: MikroORM implements the pattern literally: the UnitOfWork holds an identity map and a snapshot copy of every loaded entity, em.flush() diffs the snapshots, queues INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for exactly the changed columns, and runs them inside a database transaction, so em.transactional(cb) only has to define the boundary. Choose it when the application wants deferred writes and dirty tracking in JavaScript; the tradeoff is a heavier runtime, snapshot memory per loaded entity, and the need to learn the flush modes (COMMIT, AUTO, ALWAYS) that decide when writes escape.
pitfalls: FlushMode.ALWAYS issues writes before every query, so intermediate states reach the database and rollback no longer restores the previous picture.
The snapshot doubles the memory of every loaded entity; long-lived EntityManagers accumulate both the identity map and the snapshots.
Changes on managed entities that were never persist()ed can be missed by auto-flush heuristics, producing surprising ordering of writes.
